expectations.text: Output redirects away from NetworkX for this scale (5M nodes, 800M edges)
expectations.evidence: NetworkX is a pure-Python library that stores graphs as Python dictionaries. For a graph with 7 million nodes and 800 million edges, you are looking at roughly 60–100 GB of RAM just to hold the graph in memory — before any algorithm runs. On most machines, loading this graph into NetworkX will either exhaust memory or take hours.

expectations.text: Output recommends NetworKit, cuGraph, or graph-tool as appropriate large-scale alternatives
expectations.evidence: Comparison table explicitly lists NetworKit ('Handles billions of edges; has approximate betweenness built in'), cuGraph/RAPIDS ('Can process 800M-edge graphs in minutes on modern GPUs'), and graph-tool ('excellent for BISBM'). Summary states: 'Use NetworKit or cuGraph for scalable graph analytics.'

expectations.text: Output warns that exact betweenness centrality is computationally infeasible at this scale (O(VE) or O(V*E))
expectations.evidence: Exact betweenness centrality has time complexity O(V * E) — for your graph that is roughly 7 million × 800 million ≈ 5.6 × 10¹⁵ operations. Even on fast hardware, exact betweenness is computationally infeasible at this scale. It would take months to years to complete.

expectations.text: Output recognizes that this is a bipartite (user-item) graph and warns that running standard community detection on it would conflate user and item nodes into mixed communities
expectations.evidence: Your graph is bipartite: one partition contains users, the other contains items... Running them on the full bipartite graph will produce communities that intermix users and items arbitrarily — a community might be 'some users + some items,' which is hard to interpret and often not what you want.

expectations.text: Output mentions approximate betweenness (sampling-based) or questions whether betweenness is the right metric for a recommendation system
expectations.evidence: Both addressed: (1) 'Approximate betweenness via sampling (e.g., Brandes' algorithm with random pivot sampling). You sample k source nodes rather than all V, bringing complexity to O(k * E).' (2) 'Question whether betweenness is the right metric. In a user-item recommendation graph... For recommendation systems, degree centrality, PageRank, or item co-occurrence strength are usually more interpretable and actionable.'
